notes.h: Stress and the structures it produces
notes.b: Plate movement at boundaries produces three kinds of stress, and each kind produces a different structure.
points: Compression (pushing together) produces folds and reverse or thrust faults; it occurs where plates converge.
Tension (pulling apart) produces normal faults; it occurs where plates diverge.
Shearing (sliding past) produces tear, or strike-slip, faults; it occurs where plates slide past each other.
Rock bends into folds when compressed slowly, especially when deep, hot and under pressure.
Rock breaks, forming faults, when stress is sudden or the rock is brittle.
Compression is horizontal pressure that squeezes layers of rock into a shorter distance, so they buckle into folds.
An anticline is an upfold: layers are pushed upwards into an arch.
A syncline is a downfold: layers are pushed downwards into a trough.
The limbs are the sides of a fold; the axis is the line along its crest or trough.
Diagram: label the anticline A and the syncline B.

notes.h: Types of fold, in order of increasing compression
points: Simple (symmetrical) fold: the two limbs dip at equal angles.
Asymmetrical fold: one limb is steeper than the other.
Overfold: one limb is pushed over the other.
Recumbent fold: the folded layers lie almost flat.
Overthrust fold, or nappe: the fold breaks along a thrust fault and is pushed far forward over other rocks.
Diagram: one cross-section sketch for each of the five types, in that order.
1. Sediments are deposited in a sea lying between two converging plates.
2. The plates converge, and the sediments are compressed.
3. The sediments are folded into anticlines and synclines.
4. Continued pressure produces overfolds, recumbent folds and nappes.
5. The crust is thickened and uplifted into long, high ranges parallel to the plate edge.
Diagram: before-and-after cross-sections of the sea floor and the resulting fold mountain.
Young fold mountains, such as the Alps, are high and steep.
Old fold mountains have been worn down by hundreds of millions of years of weathering and erosion into lower, rounded mountains.
Ireland's mountains are old fold mountains, formed by Caledonian folding (north-east to south-west trend: Donegal, Mayo, Wicklow) and Armorican folding (east to west trend: Munster).
Other young fold ranges include the Himalayas, the Andes, the Rockies and the Atlas Mountains of north Africa.
The landform depends on which rocks are exposed by erosion.
In Munster, resistant sandstone survives on the anticlines as ridges.
Weaker limestone survives in the synclines as valleys.
Rivers follow the weak rock along the synclines.
Where a river breaks through a ridge, it cuts across it, giving trellised drainage and sharp right-angled bends.

notes.b: Armorican folding produced a landscape of east to west ridges and valleys.
points: Ridges of Old Red Sandstone include Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Caha Mountains.
Valleys of Carboniferous limestone include the Blackwater valley and the Lee valley.
The River Blackwater flows east along a limestone valley, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to reach the sea at Youghal.
The River Lee flows east to Cork Harbour.
The coastal ends of the valleys in Co. Cork and Kerry were drowned to form rias: Bantry Bay, Dingle Bay and the Kenmare River.
The Armorican front is the northern limit of strong Armorican folding, running east to west across Munster.
South of the front, rocks were intensely folded and pushed, or thrust, northwards.
North of the front, folding is gentle.
Alpine folding resulted from the collision of the African plate with the Eurasian plate.
Recumbent folds and nappes are characteristic of the Alps.
Mont Blanc is the highest peak of the Alps.
The Appalachian Mountains of eastern North America are old fold mountains.
They were folded in the same mountain-building episodes as Ireland's older mountains, when the two continents were joined.
The Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians show long, parallel folded ridges and valleys.
Doming pushes rock layers upwards from below into a circular or oval upfold, by compression or by rising magma.
Erosion removes the top of the dome first, exposing older rocks in the centre.
Resistant layers form rings of escarpments facing inwards towards the centre.
Drainage flows outwards from the centre in a radial pattern.
Example: the Lake District, England, with rivers and lakes radiating outwards from the centre.
Rock layers in Kent, Surrey and Sussex were pushed up into a dome, an elongated anticline.
Erosion removed the chalk from the top, exposing older sandstones and clays.
The chalk now forms the North Downs and the South Downs, two escarpments.
Clay vales lie inside the Downs, and sandstone forms the High Weald in the centre.
A fault is a fracture in the crust along which rocks have moved.
Displacement may be vertical (rocks move up or down), horizontal (rocks move sideways), or both.
Tension pulls the crust apart.
One block slides down the fault plane relative to the other, so the crust is lengthened.
Diagram: a block sliding down along a fault plane, marked as a normal fault.
Compression pushes one block up the fault plane over the other, so the crust is shortened.
A thrust fault is a low-angle reverse fault that can push rocks a long way forward, linked to nappes.
Diagram: a block pushed up and over the other along a fault plane, marked as a reverse fault.
Shearing makes blocks move horizontally past each other along a tear fault.
A transform fault is a tear fault at a plate boundary.
Examples of transform faults: the San Andreas Fault, California; the North and East Anatolian Faults, Turkey.
The shattered rock of the fault zone is eroded into a straight valley.
Ridges and rivers are offset sideways across the fault.
Example: the Great Glen Fault, Scotland, where Loch Ness lies in the straight valley eroded along it.
The Donegal tear faults run north-east to south-west.
Rivers and glaciers have eroded long, straight valleys along them.
The Gweebarra Fault and the Leannan Fault are two of them; the Gweebarra River valley follows the Gweebarra Fault.
A fault scarp is a steep slope or cliff where one block has been raised above the other.
A horst is a block raised between two parallel faults, or left standing as the land on either side sinks.
A graben, or rift valley, is a block that sinks between two parallel normal faults, forming a long, flat-floored valley with steep walls, often holding lakes.
Diagram: a fault scarp as a steep cliff between two blocks at different heights.

notes.h: How a horst and graben form
points: 1. Tension stretches the crust, producing normal faults on either side of a block.
2. The central block sinks between the faults, forming a graben.
3. The blocks on either side stand higher, forming horsts.
Diagram: horst and graben shown together in one cross-section, with the normal faults labelled.

notes.h: Rift valleys and horsts in practice
points: The Rhine rift valley, a graben, lies between the Vosges, France, and the Black Forest, Germany, which are horsts.
The East African Rift Valley includes a graben in which Lake Tanganyika lies.
The Central Lowlands of Scotland are a rift valley between the Highland Boundary Fault and the Southern Uplands Fault.
Faults help to guide the lines of coastlines and drainage.
Earthquakes occur along active faults.

keyTerms.definition: Stress that pushes rock together, producing folds and reverse or thrust faults.
Stress that pulls rock apart, producing normal faults.
Stress that makes rock slide past itself, producing tear faults.
An upfold in which layers are pushed upwards into an arch.
A downfold in which layers are pushed downwards into a trough.
A fold whose layers lie almost flat.
An overthrust fold that has broken along a thrust fault and been pushed far forward over other rocks.
The upward push of rock layers from below into a circular or oval upfold.
A fracture in the crust along which rocks have moved.
A fault caused by tension, along which one block slides down relative to the other.
A low-angle reverse fault that can push rocks a long way forward.
A fault caused by shearing, along which blocks move horizontally past each other.
A tear fault at a plate boundary.
A steep slope or cliff where one block has been raised above the other along a fault.
A block of land raised between two parallel faults, or left standing as the land on either side sinks.
A block of land that sinks between two parallel normal faults, forming a rift valley.

questions.prompt: Examine how folding influences the development of landforms, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Compression squeezes layers of rock into a shorter distance, so they buckle into folds: anticlines are upfolds and synclines are downfolds. Rocks fold when compressed slowly, especially when deep and hot, and the fold types grow more extreme with increasing compression: simple, asymmetrical, overfold, recumbent, and overthrust fold or nappe. Fold mountains form when sediments in a sea between converging plates are compressed, folded and uplifted into long ranges parallel to the plate edge. Young fold mountains, such as the Alps, with African-Eurasian plate collision, are high and steep, with recumbent folds and nappes; Mont Blanc is the highest peak. Old fold mountains have been worn down over hundreds of millions of years into lower, rounded mountains. Ireland's mountains are old, formed by Caledonian folding (north-east to south-west) and Armorican folding (east to west). In Munster, the resistant Old Red Sandstone survives on the anticlines as ridges, such as Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Caha Mountains. Weaker Carboniferous limestone survives in the synclines as valleys, such as the Blackwater and Lee valleys. Rivers follow the weak rock along the synclines and cut across the ridges where they break through, giving trellised drainage and sharp right-angled bends. The River Blackwater flows east along its valley, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin to reach the sea at Youghal. The Appalachians in eastern North America show the same pattern of long, parallel folded ridges and valleys, and are old fold mountains formed in the same episodes as Ireland's older mountains.

questions.prompt: Examine how faulting influences the development of landforms.
questions.model: Stress determines the fault type: compression produces reverse and thrust faults, tension produces normal faults, and shearing produces tear faults. Rocks break along faults when stress is sudden or the rock is brittle. A normal fault lets one block slide down the fault plane, lengthening the crust. Where tension stretches the crust, a central block can sink between two parallel normal faults to form a graben, a flat-floored rift valley with steep walls that often holds lakes; the blocks on either side stand higher as horsts. The Rhine rift valley is a graben between the Vosges, France, and the Black Forest, Germany, which are horsts. The East African Rift Valley includes a graben in which Lake Tanganyika lies. The Central Lowlands of Scotland are a rift valley between the Highland Boundary Fault and the Southern Uplands Fault. A fault scarp is a steep slope or cliff where one block has been raised above the other. A reverse fault pushes one block up the fault plane over the other, shortening the crust; a thrust fault is a low-angle reverse fault that can push rocks a long way forward. Tear faults form where blocks move horizontally past each other. Shattered rock in the fault zone erodes into straight valleys, and ridges and rivers are offset sideways across the fault. The Great Glen Fault, Scotland, is a tear fault, and Loch Ness lies in the straight valley eroded along it. In Donegal, tear faults run north-east to south-west, and rivers and glaciers have eroded long, straight valleys along them, such as the Gweebarra valley along the Gweebarra Fault. The San Andreas Fault, California, is a transform fault, a tear fault at a plate boundary. Faults also guide the lines of coastlines and drainage.

questions.prompt: With the aid of a diagram, describe and explain how fold mountains are formed.
questions.model: Diagram: a before-and-after cross-section, showing horizontal sediments deposited in a sea between two converging plates, and then folded anticlines and synclines forming a range above the sea floor. Stage 1: sediments accumulate in a sea between two plates. Stage 2: the plates converge, so the sediments are compressed horizontally. Stage 3: the layers buckle into anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds). Stage 4: continued compression produces overfolds, recumbent folds and nappes, and the nappes may break along thrust faults and be pushed far forward. Stage 5: the crust is thickened and uplifted into long, high ranges parallel to the plate edge. Irish example: Macgillycuddy's Reeks are Old Red Sandstone ridges on anticlines, formed by Armorican folding. Foreign example: the Alps, formed by the collision of the African and Eurasian plates, with recumbent folds and nappes.
